title: How to Review a SaaS Tool’s Data Practices
content:
A SaaS product may solve the work problem and still be the wrong place for the work's data. Before uploading a real document or connecting an account, map what the service will receive, how it uses that information, who can access it, and how you can remove it. This review is a practical procurement step, not a legal conclusion about every jurisdiction.

Start with the data you plan to send

List input categories rather than a vague label such as “business data.” A calendar integration may expose event titles, attendee addresses, descriptions, and historical entries. A document tool may receive file contents, metadata, comments, and names. Identify whether data includes customer records, credentials, source code, regulated information, or public material. Record the minimum fields the task actually needs.

The US Federal Trade Commission's business guidance recommends taking stock of personal information, keeping only what is needed, protecting it, disposing of it appropriately, and planning for incidents. That guidance is a useful review frame, though it does not determine your organization's legal obligations. Apply it to the integration: could the tool work with redacted samples, narrower permissions, or a separate test workspace?

Draw the data flow from source to vendor, subprocessor if disclosed, exports, backups, logs, and deletion route. A vendor's main storage region is not a complete map if support staff, analytics services, or embedded AI features process the same content elsewhere. Ask what the service collects automatically through telemetry and what the user deliberately uploads. Separate account metadata from customer content where the contract does.

Read the actual product commitments

Read the current privacy notice, data processing terms, security documentation, and service-specific feature terms. Save the version or access date. Marketing pages may summarize these documents but can omit exceptions. Look for retention periods, deletion timing, backup treatment, support access, breach notification, subprocessors, and whether content is used to improve models or products. Record exact passages and unresolved questions for the vendor.

NIST SP 800-144 discusses security and privacy considerations when organizations outsource data, applications, and infrastructure to public clouds. Its publication is older, so treat it as a risk framework rather than a statement about a current vendor's features. The operational lesson is that outsourcing changes control boundaries; it does not remove your need to know what information leaves your environment and which controls are shared.

Check the service's identity and access model. Can you require multifactor authentication, restrict third-party app scopes, remove former members, and audit administrative actions? Does a connector request read-only access when it only needs to search, or does it request write and delete permissions? Confirm in the real authorization screen, not only in a setup guide. Broad scopes can be acceptable for some functions, but the reason should be explicit and reviewable.

Test claims with a safe trial

Use synthetic or cleared sample data for initial setup. Verify which permissions the integration asks for and what remains after disconnecting. Attempt an export and a deletion in a test workspace; note whether each action is immediate, queued, or subject to backup retention. A successful UI click does not prove all copies are gone, so compare observed behavior with contractual commitments and ask for clarification where needed.

Review incident evidence without reducing the decision to a badge. A security certification or audit report can support a particular control claim, but its scope and date matter. Does it cover the exact product, region, and feature you plan to use? Is the report available under appropriate terms? Do not claim a vendor is “secure” because one document exists. Record the specific controls that matter for your data and the evidence you actually inspected.

Consider exit before adoption. Can you export work in a useful format? How will you revoke integration tokens and remove users? Which records must be retained for your own operations, and how will you preserve them before deletion? A tool that cannot return your data or explain deletion may create a lock-in cost larger than its subscription fee. Assign an internal owner for periodic review when vendor terms or product features change.

Hypothetical example: a meeting-summary service

Suppose a hypothetical team wants a service that summarizes client meetings. The proposed calendar connector requests access to all historical event descriptions, while the pilot only needs meetings in one test calendar. The privacy notice explains general retention but the product page does not clearly state whether transcript content is used for model improvement. The team records both gaps before connecting live accounts.

They test with a synthetic meeting, ask the vendor to clarify content use and deletion, and compare a narrower manual-upload option. They may approve only the test calendar while the questions remain open. This is an illustrative decision, not an assessment of a real vendor. The important move is to narrow data exposure to the use case while unresolved commitments are investigated.

Checklist for a review record

  • Describe the planned task and minimum data fields.
  • Inventory personal, confidential, and public data separately.
  • Read current service terms, retention, deletion, and subprocessor details.
  • Confirm actual integration scopes and administrative controls.
  • Test export and deletion with synthetic data.
  • Record evidence, open vendor questions, and approved boundaries.
  • Name an owner and a review trigger for material changes.

The strongest review is proportionate and specific. It names what the tool may process, what evidence supports that decision, and which questions remain unanswered. That record helps a team use a useful service without treating a polished interface as a substitute for data stewardship.
excerpt: Review a SaaS tool by mapping the exact data it receives, reading current commitments, testing permissions and deletion, and recording approved boundaries.
